title: The Personal vs the Systemic: Parenting Realities Within Racist Societies
author: Tabitha St. Bernard-Jacobs and Adam St. Bernard Jacobs
summary: Antiracist parenting educators Tabitha St. Bernard-Jacobs and Adam St. Bernard Jacobs respond to Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay in alternating voices, declining to judge her choices and insisting that Black and Brown parents face impossible options for which the system must be held accountable. Adam, who worked across New York City schools and helped launch a community school, recalls how her 2016 essay shaped his colleagues' work. They offer three reflections: racism is systemic but must still be addressed at individual and institutional levels, raising justice-minded children is an experiment with no true experts, and white parents and Black and Brown parents should read the essay differently. White parents are urged to support neighboring schools, build coalitions, and do antiracist work at home. The authors conclude that Black children face inequity in both predominantly white and predominantly Black schools, and they hope readers turn reflection into action.
points: The authors present Hannah-Jones's story as evidence that even a privileged Black parent cannot solve systemic racism through individual choice.
Tabitha describes the stress and health costs Black and Brown parents bear in combating racism daily.
Parenting is framed as a researched experiment in which each child is a one-of-one prototype.
White parents are urged to support under-resourced PTAs at other schools, attend board meetings, and parent against racism at home.
Black children, they argue, face identity and racism challenges in white schools and resource disparities in Black schools.
quotes: I applaud Hannah-Jones for the bravery it took to release all of this from within her, with full knowledge that the anti-DEI, segregation voices are poised to weaponize this against us all.
Black and Brown parents face impossible choices. We have to hold the system accountable for this and try not to turn on each other.
Even though one family or one school may seek to do better, they exist within a system that deprioritizes our Black and Brown children and, in many cases, causes them real harm.

Each kid is a brand new prototype of themselves. They’re 1 of 1. And each parent is trying to figure out the best way to raise this new human with new stages every other day while we ourselves experience life in new ways.
Do the work needed so Black and Brown parents don’t have to make the impossible choices that Hannah-Jones had to make for her daughter.
The grim reality is that no matter where Black and Brown kids attend school in the United States, they will face inequity and racism.
